planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring once nights stay reliably above 50F, in full sun on deep, rich, well-drained soil; this lowland Honduran species has less cold tolerance than the higher-elevation Mexican Dioons and needs a genuinely frost-free, warm site.

directions: Dioon mejiae hails from the seasonally dry pine-oak foothills of Olancho and the Mosquitia region of Honduras, where it forms one of the largest trunks in the genus and carries a dense crown of broad, leathery, yellow-green to olive fronds. It is used locally as a source of starch from its seeds and pith, much like Dioon edule in Mexico, but in gardens it is grown purely as a bold specimen plant for warm, frost-free landscapes. Give it more regular moisture through the growing season than the drier-adapted Mexican species, since its native range receives a distinct summer wet season, while keeping the soil on the drier side through winter. Because it comes from consistently warm lowland habitat, it is markedly more cold-sensitive than Dioon edule or D. merolae and should be reserved for the mildest zone 10-11 gardens or grown in a large container that can be sheltered.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in bright shade under a tree canopy, in loose, humus-rich, well-drained soil; this understory species is more shade-loving and slightly more cold-tolerant than most cultivated Ceratozamia.

directions: Ceratozamia hildae grows on the shaded floor of limestone cloud forest in San Luis Potosi and Queretaro, Mexico, sending up soft, glossy, deep-green leaflets on long, gently drooping fronds that emerge in a pale, almost translucent flush before hardening off. Its trunk stays essentially subterranean, so mature plants read as a low, spreading clump of fine-textured foliage rather than an upright cycad silhouette, and the narrow, closely spaced leaflets give it a distinctly soft, almost bamboo-like texture unlike the stiffer leaves of most cycads. It tolerates brief light freezes better than many tropical cycads thanks to its higher-elevation origin, but it still wants steady shade and evenly moist, fast-draining soil to look its best. Its fine texture makes it a natural companion for ferns and other shade-garden foliage rather than a stand-alone architectural specimen.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in partial to full shade in rich, well-drained, humus-heavy soil; this Tamaulipas cloud-forest cycad needs steady humidity and protection from hot, direct sun.

directions: Native to the cloud forests of Tamaulipas in northeastern Mexico, Ceratozamia kuesteriana forms a low, mostly underground stem topped with arching fronds of glossy, dark green leaflets that are broader and more strongly ribbed than those of the finer-textured Ceratozamia hildae. It is one of the more forgiving Ceratozamia species in cultivation, adapting to typical shade-garden conditions as long as it is kept out of harsh midday sun and given soil that never stays soggy. Offsets occasionally form at the base, slowly building a multi-crowned clump over many years. Give it a permanently shaded position under high tree canopy or shade cloth, since even brief exposure to strong sun tends to bleach and scorch the leaflets.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to light shade on well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil; this monsoonal Australian species tolerates a distinct wet-dry seasonal cycle better than constant year-round irrigation.

directions: Cycas media ranges across the monsoonal woodlands of northern Australia and parts of New Guinea and the southwestern Pacific, building an eventually tall, solitary trunk topped with a dense crown of stiff, deep-green leaflets. It is adapted to a sharply seasonal climate with a wet summer growing period followed by a long, dry winter, so it appreciates generous moisture from spring through early fall but should be kept much drier once growth slows. Its overall size and habit sit between the compact Cycas siamensis and the larger Cycas circinalis, making it a versatile mid-sized trunking cycad for open, sunny plantings in the warmest zones. Established plants handle poor, sandy soils and periodic drought stress well, reflecting the open savanna country where it naturally grows.
sources: Kew Science -- Plants of the World Online: Cycas media

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in bright shade in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil; this rainforest-floor species from Nicaragua and Costa Rica has no cold tolerance and needs steady warmth and humidity year-round.

directions: Zamia splendens grows on the shaded floor of lowland rainforest in Nicaragua and Costa Rica, where its arching leaflets often carry a subtle silvery-blue to olive sheen and prominent pale veining that give the foliage an almost pewter-like shimmer in dappled light. The stem stays short and mostly subterranean, so the plant reads as a low rosette of patterned leaves rather than a trunking specimen, distinguishing it in scale and color from the broader, plain-green leaflets of Zamia skinneri. It depends on constant warmth, humidity, and filtered light, and will scorch quickly if moved into open sun or allowed to dry out for extended periods. Among collectors it is valued specifically for its foliage color, making it a striking textural accent in a shaded tropical border or large humid container planting.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to light shade in lean, sandy, fast-draining soil; this diminutive Cuban species is one of the smallest cultivated cycads and suits pots and rock-garden pockets far better than open beds.

directions: Zamia pygmaea is native to sandy coastal savanna and scrub on Cuba and the Isla de la Juventud, where it stays remarkably small even at maturity, rarely reaching more than a few narrow leaflets on short, stiff fronds arising from an almost entirely buried, tuber-like caudex. Its diminutive stature makes it one of the smallest true cycads in cultivation, well suited to shallow pots, bonsai-style displays, or tucked into rock-garden crevices where a full-sized Zamia would overwhelm the composition. It tolerates lean, sandy, fast-draining soil and considerable drought once established, reflecting the exposed, well-drained coastal ground of its native range, and rots quickly if kept in rich or constantly wet soil. Give it a warm, frost-free spot in full sun to light shade and treat it as a slow, long-lived collector's curiosity rather than a fast-growing landscape plant.
sources: IUCN/SSC Cycad Specialist Group Red List

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun on well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in zone 9-11; this escarpment species tolerates brief cool spells better than lowland tropical cycads but still needs sharp drainage.

directions: Encephalartos lebomboensis takes its name from the Lebombo Mountains along the border of South Africa, Eswatini, and Mozambique, where it grows on steep, rocky, quartzitic slopes in open bushveld. It develops a solitary, moderately thick trunk crowned by rigid, dark bluish-green leaflets that are less twisted and dramatically spined than those of Encephalartos horridus, giving it a tidier, more upright profile suited to formal specimen planting. Established plants handle periodic drought and lean, rocky soil well, mirroring the sparse escarpment habitat where it naturally occurs, and it has been propagated in specialty cycad nurseries for decades. Give it excellent drainage and full sun, and expect a slow but steady increase in trunk height over many years.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun on deep, well-drained soil in zone 9-11; this is one of the tallest-growing Macrozamia species and needs long-term space for a substantial trunk.

directions: Macrozamia moorei grows on the semi-arid inland plains and open woodland of central Queensland, where old specimens develop one of the tallest, most massive trunks of any cycad in Australia, dwarfing the low, mostly stemless habit of the more familiar Macrozamia communis. Its stiff, gray-green fronds form a broad, rounded crown atop the trunk, and the plant tolerates considerably more heat, drought, and lean soil than most cultivated cycads once it is established. Growth is exceedingly slow, so a garden specimen represents a multi-generational investment toward the towering form seen in old wild populations. Give it full sun, sharp drainage, and plenty of overhead and lateral room to accommodate its eventual size.
sources: Kew Science -- Plants of the World Online: Macrozamia moorei

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in bright shade under canopy in rich, humus-heavy, well-drained soil; this narrow-range Queensland species needs the same shaded, humid conditions as Bowenia spectabilis but has distinctly toothed leaflet margins.

directions: Bowenia serrulata is a narrow-range endemic of the Byfield area on the central Queensland coast, where it grows as an understory plant in dry rainforest and eucalypt woodland with a wholly subterranean, tuber-like stem. Its bipinnate fronds carry finely toothed, or serrulate, leaflet margins that distinguish it at a glance from the smooth-edged leaflets of the more widespread Bowenia spectabilis, though the two species share a similar low, spreading, fern-like silhouette. Grow it in the same steady shade and humus-rich, well-drained soil as its relative, since both come from similar forest-floor conditions and have no tolerance for open sun or cold. Its restricted native range and distinctive foliage texture make it a worthwhile companion planting alongside Bowenia spectabilis for collectors wanting the full genus.
sources: Kew Science -- Plants of the World Online: Bowenia serrulata

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade on deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil in zone 10-11; this rainforest giant needs high humidity, steady warmth, and eventually a great deal of overhead and lateral space.

directions: Lepidozamia hopei is native to the tropical rainforests of far north Queensland's Atherton Tablelands and Cape York, where wild specimens develop the tallest trunk of any cycad species on Earth, occasionally exceeding 60 feet after many centuries of growth. Its long, glossy, dark-green fronds are broadly similar to those of the more commonly grown Lepidozamia peroffskyana, but the species ultimately builds a taller, more slender trunk and demands consistently higher humidity and warmth to thrive. Growth is extremely slow even by cycad standards, so in cultivation it is grown and appreciated chiefly as a young to medium-sized specimen rather than for any realistic prospect of reaching its wild stature. Give it filtered light, rich well-drained soil, and shelter from both direct hot sun and any hint of cold, since it has essentially no frost tolerance.
sources: Kew Science -- Plants of the World Online: Lepidozamia hopei
